added_claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
added_claims.quote: what you saw around liberation day was three days in a row of extensive shocks, not one and then a quiet period and then a reversal
added_claims.claim: Liberation Day was three consecutive days of extreme moves (by turbulence metrics), not one shock followed by calm and a reversal, which made it a hard signal for price-trend and vol-sizing models; managers whose vol estimate forgot the shock faster coped better.
added_claims.direction: faster vol estimation improves response to consecutive-day shocks
added_claims.conditions: Shock clusters of several days; opposite in 2022 when speed hurt.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare vol-estimate half-life with returns around the shock

added_claims.speaker: Nick Balters
added_claims.quote: We literally just ranked anywhere from like know two month to a 12 month halfife
added_claims.claim: Nick's year-by-year study ranks trend speeds from 2 to 12 month half-lives across three universe sizes (about 10 markets, a few mid-size, and 80+ markets) for each of 25 years, which is how he finds that the slowest speed and a small universe won in 2023-25.
added_claims.indicator: trend half-life (2-12 months) by universe size, 25-year calendar-year ranking
added_claims.conditions: Calendar-year ranking of speeds and universes; depends on the chosen universes.
added_claims.testable: yes - the ranking exercise is replicable

added_claims.speaker: Nick Balters
added_claims.quote: It happened however that still a smaller universe was was was a better one to
added_claims.claim: Even in 2022, when the fastest speed was best, a smaller concentrated universe still beat the larger ones, so the small-universe advantage held across 2022-25 while the best speed switched from fastest to slowest.
added_claims.conditions: 2022-25 only; the long-run record may differ (see Andrew and Katie on the 25-year view).
added_claims.testable: yes - same calendar-year ranking

added_claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
added_claims.quote: it's hard to find capacity for non-correlated assets
added_claims.claim: Capacity is the constraint: there is little room in genuinely non-correlated assets, so the key question is how infrastructure and liquidity will be built (and what else can be seen as non-correlated) to absorb the inflows.
added_claims.indicator: capacity of non-correlated assets and strategies
added_claims.conditions: Because early adopters are arriving faster than infrastructure.
added_claims.testable: partly - capacity is hard to measure

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they now have a bucket now they've had to figure out how to fill it
added_claims.claim: Allocators have created an alternatives bucket after 2022 but now have to work out what to put in it, so demand for products that fill the bucket (futures-based ETFs, replication, trend) is limited by knowledge, not by desire.
added_claims.conditions: Education is gradual.
added_claims.testable: no - qualitative demand driver

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: that's why Goldman just paid 2 billion for Innovator
added_claims.claim: Buffered and defined-outcome ETFs are an early-stage growth area in a 13 trillion dollar ETF market, evidenced by Goldman paying about 2 billion dollars for Innovator.
added_claims.indicator: buffered ETF market, Goldman acquisition of Innovator
added_claims.conditions: Data point supporting the 'still early' view.
added_claims.testable: yes - the deal and AUM are public

added_claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
added_claims.quote: imbalance between uh people needing non-correlation and the amount of non-correlation available um that is maybe the most important thing to understand in finance
added_claims.claim: Jim's core thesis: flows into precious metals, crypto, structured products and hedge funds are driven by a supply and demand imbalance between investors needing non-correlation and the amount of it available.
added_claims.direction: non-correlated assets and strategies attract flows
added_claims.conditions: Holds while long assets and bonds fail to offset equity risk.
added_claims.testable: partly - flow data can be compared with correlations

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: I wonder if this will actually change the fee compression at some point that we've seen because there might uh you know more demand for the best uh strategies
added_claims.claim: Niels asks whether rising demand for non-correlation will end fee compression for the best strategies; Alan's answer is that supply and demand already lifts fees for scarce managers.
added_claims.indicator: manager fees vs demand for non-correlation
added_claims.conditions: Applies to managers in short supply.
added_claims.testable: yes - fee levels by strategy type over time

added_claims.speaker: Jim Kasang
added_claims.quote: these things are actually going to be the primary driver at some point of the underlying assets themselves
added_claims.claim: If inflows into structured products and hedge funds keep growing, their positioning could become the primary driver of underlying asset behaviour, which could be a structural risk to correlations and liquidity in future years.
added_claims.indicator: structured product and hedge fund flow impact on markets
added_claims.conditions: Depends on continued growth of these flows (his thesis, not shown).
added_claims.testable: partly - flow impact on volatility and dispersion can be studied

added_claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
added_claims.quote: when you have a 20% difference between one product and another
added_claims.claim: With about 20% spread between trend products in a year, every manager takes a turn at the bad end, so investor education about dispersion is needed for the industry to grow.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to investor adoption.
added_claims.testable: yes - dispersion by year

added_claims.speaker: Katie Kaminski
added_claims.quote: most of the assets are really in the institutional space
added_claims.claim: Managed-futures assets sit mostly with institutions; ETFs and other wrappers are widening access to a different investor universe that has not held these strategies before.
added_claims.conditions: Katie cites her paper from last year.
added_claims.testable: yes - AUM by investor type

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: can recognize the statistical benefits of a 3 or 5% allocation to the strategy but does not want to spend a year getting up to up the learning curve
added_claims.claim: A product niche exists for model-portfolio allocators who see the statistical benefit of a 3-5% managed-futures sleeve but will not spend a year learning how to evaluate dispersion; a replication ETF serves them.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to model allocators without a manager-selection function.
added_claims.testable: no - description of a client segment

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: people who will view dispersion as a huge positive because it allows them to make you know allows them to pick somebody who did well last year
added_claims.claim: Some investors treat dispersion as an opportunity to pick last year's winner or drop laggards and reconfigure; others want a simple beta-like solution, so products must fit different preference functions.
added_claims.conditions: The first style risks return-chasing (see Katie's point on investor outcomes).
added_claims.testable: partly - evidence on return-chasing exists

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: this space has has a a perception of a lot of randomness
added_claims.claim: In some hedge fund categories allocators believe in identifiable star managers, but trend following is seen as random, so luck and skill are hard to separate and the answer investors want is skill.
added_claims.conditions: The narrative problem is in separating luck from skill.
added_claims.testable: no - perception

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: managers who became very popular only to see their AUM implode uh in the following years
added_claims.claim: Niels recalls cases over the last decade or two of managers who became very popular and then lost most of their assets, a bad outcome for the underlying investor, which supports the argument that performance chasing hurts.
added_claims.conditions: Anecdotal; no names given.
added_claims.testable: yes - AUM flows vs subsequent returns

added_claims.speaker: Rich Brennan
added_claims.quote: I inevitably find when people say that it's from a position of hindsight um so it's very easy from that position to actually say something's very obvious
added_claims.claim: Claims that a design decision was obvious come from hindsight; every design involves trade-offs and uncertainty, so the future should be treated as unknown rather than relying on the regime that just worked.
added_claims.conditions: Contrasts with Andrew's observation that managers present choices with confidence.
added_claims.testable: no - epistemic point

added_claims.speaker: Yov Git
added_claims.quote: holding a CTA is actually very difficult because you know it's a sharp one strategy maybe a little bit less maybe a little bit more um and it's kind of difficult to to sit within my IC
added_claims.claim: A CTA is hard to hold in an investment committee because a Sharpe-about-1 strategy has losing years and the committee asks why it lost money, so a mix of CTA types can make the allocation easier to hold.
added_claims.indicator: CTA Sharpe ratio, investment committee patience
added_claims.conditions: Applies to institutions with committee oversight.
added_claims.testable: partly - depends on the Sharpe and loss frequency

added_claims.speaker: Yov Git
added_claims.quote: it actually gives the investor a true choice and also clarity about when each of these component is likely to perform
added_claims.claim: If trend programs state different objectives and target distinct risk factors, investors can see when each component should perform, gain confidence, and hold each through its expected off-periods.
added_claims.indicator: trend program objectives and risk factors
added_claims.conditions: Requires managers to state objectives.
added_claims.testable: partly - behaviour and retention are hard to test

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: would have predicted the outcome that that Nick laid out in terms of very very long-term models work
added_claims.claim: No one four years ago would have predicted that very slow models on major markets would win for three years, which is why design winners are unforecastable, while allocators look for a manager who says 'I knew that would happen'.
added_claims.direction: slow models and small universe won 2023-25
added_claims.conditions: Hindsight: unforeseeable at the time.
added_claims.testable: no - narrative point

added_claims.speaker: Alan Dunn
added_claims.quote: you've got other biases career risk very hard to defend you know an underperforming manager
added_claims.claim: Manager selection is distorted by after-the-fact narratives for whoever is doing well, recency bias and career risk (it is hard to defend an underperformer), so investors judge on short performance despite the long data needed.
added_claims.conditions: Applies to allocators and investment committees.
added_claims.testable: partly - behavioural finance evidence

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: Are we talking about what a statistician would call a test against a hypothesis of zero returns?
added_claims.claim: The data needed depends on the test: showing a manager's return is positive (zero hypothesis) needs less data than showing they beat a benchmark by a stated margin, so allocators should specify the hypothesis before asking how long.
added_claims.indicator: statistical test design for manager evaluation
added_claims.conditions: A 20% outperformer is found quickly; a 50bp outperformer takes much longer.
added_claims.testable: yes - power calculation

added_claims.speaker: Rob Carver
added_claims.quote: the more dispersion is in the industry, the harder it is to say whether people are outperforming other people
added_claims.claim: Greater dispersion across the industry makes it harder to tell managers apart statistically because the differences look random, which links dispersion to longer evaluation periods.
added_claims.conditions: Lower correlation between managers means more data.
added_claims.testable: yes - from correlations and tracking error

added_claims.speaker: Yov Git
added_claims.quote: what aspects of your trading you can actually improve on. Is it execution? Is it risk management
added_claims.claim: After three difficult years investors ask how a manager responds to a drawdown while staying true to trend following; the acceptable answers are improvements to execution, data and risk management, not a drift away from the core approach.
added_claims.conditions: Winton is the example of drift away from the core and back.
added_claims.testable: no - qualitative due-diligence criterion

added_claims.speaker: Nick Balters
added_claims.quote: maybe dispersion becomes a better theme but there is no particular reason to actually feel that tomorrow you know investors become risk loving
added_claims.claim: Large structured-product demand can shift where the volatility premium is best harvested (dispersion may become a better expression), but investors are not becoming risk-loving, so the premium for providing insurance remains.
added_claims.conditions: Depends on structured-product flows.
added_claims.testable: partly - dispersion vs index vol premia are observable

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: we've seen a drift from performance only from performance related uh pay to um you know flat management fee
added_claims.claim: CTA fee structures have drifted from performance-related pay toward flat management fees; some allocators prefer low flat fees (ETFs, QIS), while others want managers to take performance fees and have skin in the game.
added_claims.conditions: Allocator preference differs.
added_claims.testable: partly - fee data

corrections.issue: Attributed to Andrew Beer, but the passage comes from a panelist before Niels says 'Yeah, Andrew, you raised ...'; Andrew speaks only afterwards (and about replication concentration). Speaker is unidentified in the captions.
corrections.fix: Unidentified panelist (not Andrew Beer): a portfolio of just gold, oil and corn would have trended best in 2025 idiosyncratically, which is not true over a 25-year history, so market-selection gains in 2025 were specific to the year.

completeness_estimate: 0.78 - first reader caught each speaker's main thesis and the statistics; missed several supporting mechanisms (three-day shock structure, study method, capacity and supply-demand thesis, Katie/Andrew on investor segments, hindsight, hypothesis choice, fee drift) and mislabelled one speaker (no speaker labels in the caption).
